verses.context: The scene shifts from Bethel to the far end of Jacob's flight. The narrator compresses hundreds of miles into a single sentence and hurries Jacob to the land of the people of the east, because what matters is not the road but where God's promise at Bethel (28:15) brings him.
verses.grammar: The Hebrew says literally that Jacob ‘lifted up his feet’ (vayyissa raglav) and went, an unusual idiom for setting out. Many commentators hear in it a new vigor after the vision at Bethel: the fugitive who lay down alone with a stone for a pillow now walks on briskly. The same verb, nasa (‘lift’), returns in verse 11 when Jacob ‘lifts his voice’ and weeps, framing his arrival with two liftings. Qedem (‘east’) can also mean ‘front’ or ‘ancient times’; in the phrase bene qedem it names the peoples beyond the Jordan and the desert.
verses.history: The ‘people of the east’ (bene qedem) is a loose biblical name for the tribes and peoples east of Israel. Gideon fights them as raiders alongside the Midianites (Judges 6:3), Job is called the greatest of them (Job 1:3), and Solomon's wisdom is said to surpass theirs (1 Kings 4:30). Haran lay to the northeast of Canaan, so the term here describes the region broadly rather than pointing due east.

verses.context: Jacob sees a well, three waiting flocks, and a great stone over the well's mouth. Verse 3 pauses the action to explain the local custom, and the explanation sets up everything that follows: the stone is meant to be moved by many hands, at the proper time.
verses.grammar: Verse 2 twice uses vehinneh (‘and look’), which moves the reader behind Jacob's eyes so that we see the well and the flocks as he sees them. Verse 3 then switches to a chain of consecutive perfects (ne'esfu, ‘they would be gathered’; galalu, ‘they would roll’; hishqu, ‘they would water’; heshivu, ‘they would put back’). In narrative this form marks repeated, customary action, which is why the BSB says the shepherds "would roll away the stone". The verse describes what always happened, so that the reader will notice when Jacob does something different.
verses.history: In dry pastureland a well was a shared asset, and covering it protected the water from dust, animals, and theft. A stone too heavy for one person enforced the agreement that no shepherd would draw before the others arrived. Disputes over wells run through the patriarchal stories (Genesis 21:25, 26:18-22), which shows how much depended on them.

verses.context: A short exchange at the well tells Jacob, and the reader, that he has arrived exactly where he needed to be. Three questions bring three answers, and the last answer turns into an announcement: Laban's daughter Rachel is coming.
verses.grammar: Jacob's courteous "My brothers" (achai) uses the ordinary word for brother in its wider sense of fellow or kinsman, the same range the word will have in verses 12 and 15. The question "Is he well?" is literally ‘Is there shalom to him?’, the standard inquiry after someone's welfare; shalom covers health, safety, and prosperity together. The shepherds' reply ends with vehinneh again and a participle, ba'ah, ‘is coming’: Rachel is already approaching while they speak. Her name, Rachel, is also the Hebrew word for a ewe (Isaiah 53:7 uses it of the sheep before her shearers), fitting for the woman who first appears leading her father's flock.
verses.text: The Hebrew calls Laban ‘son of Nahor’ (ben nachor). He was in fact Nahor's grandson, the son of Bethuel (Genesis 24:24, 29), and Hebrew ben regularly means a descendant as well as a son. The BSB writes "grandson" to make the relationship clear; other translations keep the literal ‘son’.

verses.context: Jacob, a stranger for all of five minutes, tells the local shepherds how to run their day. Their answer explains again that the stone waits for all the flocks. The little dispute keeps the shepherds at the well long enough to witness what Jacob does next.
verses.grammar: "It is still broad daylight" renders ‘the day is still great’ (od hayyom gadol), an idiom for the sun being high. Jacob's three plural imperatives (‘water’, ‘go’, ‘pasture’) are brisk commands, and some commentators suspect he wants the shepherds gone before Rachel arrives. The shepherds reply lo nukhal, "We cannot". The verb yakhol usually concerns ability, but here the limit is custom and agreement rather than strength, which makes Jacob's solo effort in verse 10 all the more pointed.

verses.context: Rachel arrives while Jacob is still talking, and at the sight of her he rolls the stone off the well by himself and waters her flock. The scene echoes Genesis 24, where Rebekah appeared at a well before the servant had finished praying; now Rebekah's son meets her niece at a well.
verses.grammar: Verse 9 opens with a circumstantial clause, odennu medabber (‘he was still speaking’), a participle that sets Rachel's arrival inside Jacob's conversation, just as 24:15 set Rebekah's arrival inside the servant's prayer. Verse 10 repeats the phrase "his mother's brother" three times in one sentence: Rachel is the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, the sheep are the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, and he waters the sheep of Laban his mother's brother (the BSB smooths the third into "his uncle"). The repetition keeps Rebekah in view; this is her family, the place she sent him. The verbs vayyiggash, vayyagel, vayyashq (‘he approached, he rolled, he watered’) come in a quick run, and vayyashq (‘he watered’) sounds very close to vayyishaq (‘he kissed’) in the next verse.
verses.history: Robert Alter, in The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981), named this kind of scene the ‘betrothal type-scene’: a man travels to a foreign land, meets a young woman at a well, water is drawn, she hurries home with the news, and a marriage follows. Genesis 24 (Rebekah), this chapter (Rachel), and Exodus 2:15-21 (Zipporah) all follow the pattern, each with its own variations. In Genesis 24 the woman waters the stranger's camels; here, as later with Moses, the man waters the flock, and Jacob does it alone, by main strength.

verses.context: Jacob kisses Rachel, weeps aloud, and only then tells her who he is. His tears are the first strong emotion the narrator gives him; the man who left home alone and in danger has found his mother's people. Rachel runs home with the news, as Rebekah once ran home to her mother's household (24:28).
verses.grammar: "Wept aloud" is literally ‘lifted up his voice and wept’ (vayyissa et-qolo vayyevk), the phrase Esau used in his grief over the lost blessing (27:38). Jacob tells Rachel he is her father's achi, ‘brother’, which the BSB rightly renders "relative": Hebrew uses the word for nephews, cousins, and kinsmen as well as brothers, as when Abram calls his nephew Lot "brothers" in 13:8. The two parallel clauses with ki (‘that he was her father's relative, and that he was Rebekah's son’) give the credentials that will open Laban's door.

verses.context: Laban runs out, embraces and kisses Jacob, and brings him home; Jacob tells his whole story, and Laban claims him as his own flesh. After a month the welcome will turn into a negotiation. The reader who remembers Genesis 24 knows that Laban also ran out to meet Abraham's servant, after he had seen the gold ring and bracelets (24:29-30).
verses.grammar: Laban's verbs are emphatic: he ran, he embraced (a Piel, vaychabbeq), he kissed (another Piel, vaynashsheq), he brought him in. The warmth is real on the surface, but the echo of 24:30 hangs over it, and this time the visitor has no camels and no gold (32:10). Laban's words, "You are indeed my own flesh and blood", are literally ‘surely my bone and my flesh are you’ (akh atsmi uvesari attah), the kinship formula first heard in Adam's cry over the woman (2:23) and later used by the tribes who come to make David king (2 Samuel 5:1). The phrase chodesh yamim, ‘a month of days’, means a full month.

verses.context: A month into his stay, Laban turns kinship into employment. He sounds generous, refusing to let a relative work for nothing, but his question sets the terms of the next twenty years: Jacob will be a hired man, and Laban will set the wages.
verses.grammar: The verb avad (‘serve, work’) enters here and becomes the key word of the Haran chapters; it appears again and again in this chapter and returns in Jacob's bitter summary in 31:41. The irony is sharp: the oracle before Jacob's birth said the older would serve the younger (25:23), and now the younger is the one who serves. Maskoret ("wages") appears only here and in 31:7 and 31:41, where Jacob complains that Laban changed his wages ten times. Chinnam (‘for nothing, free’) frames the question, and the rest of the story shows who was really working for nothing.

theology.note: Laban is right that work deserves wages, and Israel's law later insists on it (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). But the chapter shows how a fair-sounding arrangement can become a means of exploitation when one party holds all the power, a concern the prophets return to (Jeremiah 22:13).

verses.context: The narrator stops the negotiation to introduce Laban's two daughters. The pause is essential to the plot: before Jacob names his price, the reader must know there are two sisters, which is older, and which one Jacob would choose.
verses.grammar: The daughters are called haggedolah and haqqetannah, literally ‘the big one’ and ‘the small one’, the ordinary Hebrew for older and younger. These are the same two adjectives used of Esau and Jacob when Rebekah dressed ‘her older son’s’ clothes on ‘her younger son’ (27:15). The words that described Jacob's deception now describe the sisters, and verse 26 will turn them against him. Rachel is yefat toar vifat mareh, ‘beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance’; the same pair of phrases in the masculine describes her son Joseph in 39:6. Leah's name is sometimes connected with a word for a wild cow, and Rachel's means ‘ewe’, but the derivation of Leah is uncertain and the narrator makes nothing of it.

verses.context: Jacob, who owns nothing, offers seven years of labor for Rachel and names her precisely: the younger daughter, Rachel. Laban agrees in words that sound like consent but never quite promise what Jacob asked.
verses.grammar: Jacob's offer is carefully specific, "your younger daughter Rachel", as if he suspects a man like Laban might need every loophole closed. Laban's answer is a comparison built on two infinitives: tov titti otah lakh mittitti otah le'ish acher, ‘better my giving her to you than my giving her to another man’. He never says ‘I will give you Rachel’, and he never uses her name. The pronoun ‘her’ stands in for the woman Jacob named, and Laban will exploit the gap. His closing imperative, shevah immadi ("Stay here with me"), binds Jacob to his household.
verses.history: A marriage in the ancient Near East normally involved a payment from the groom or his family to the bride's family, which Israel's law calls the mohar (Exodus 22:16-17; compare David in 1 Samuel 18:25). Jacob, a fugitive with only his staff, pays in labor instead. Laban's preference for a kinsman over an outsider reflects the same concern for marriage within the family that sent Abraham's servant, and then Jacob himself, to Haran (24:3-4, 28:1-2).

verses.context: One sentence covers seven years. The narrator gives no events from them, only how they felt to Jacob, and the verse is the tenderest line about love between a man and a woman in Genesis.
verses.grammar: "A few days" translates yamim achadim, the same phrase Rebekah used when she told Jacob to stay with Laban ‘for a while’ until Esau's anger cooled (27:44). Rebekah's ‘few days’ has already stretched to seven years and will become twenty (31:41). The phrase "in his eyes" (be'enav, rendered "it seemed") marks the whole comparison as Jacob's perception. The noun ahavah ("love") with the suffix, ‘in his love for her’, gives the cause: love shortened the time.

theology.note: The verse shows love willingly bearing cost. Jacob's service is not a burden resented but a price gladly paid, a human picture of the self-giving love Scripture describes as strong as death (Song of Solomon 8:6-7).

verses.context: The seven years are up and Jacob asks for his wife in blunt terms. Laban, who has had the whole time to raise any difficulty, raises none.
verses.grammar: Havah ("Grant me", ‘give’) is an imperative with an added syllable that often gives urgency, and "my wife" (ishti) shows that Jacob regards the betrothal as settled. The reason clause "for my time is complete" is literally ‘for my days are filled’ (male'u yamai). The verb male (‘fill, complete’) returns in verses 27 and 28 when Laban tells Jacob to ‘fill out’ Leah's wedding week: Jacob's completed term is answered by another term to complete.

verses.context: Laban throws a feast for the whole place, and under cover of evening brings Leah to Jacob instead of Rachel. Verse 24 interrupts at the worst possible moment with a detail about a maidservant, as if the narrator lets the trick happen while looking the other way.
verses.grammar: Laban ‘gathered’ (vayye'esof) the men of the place, the same verb used of the flocks gathering at the well (verses 3, 7, 8). The public gathering hides a private fraud: everyone is present to witness a wedding whose bride is not the one agreed. Mishteh ("feast") comes from the verb for drinking, and some interpreters suggest that wine helped the deception. The verbs in verse 23 are stark and all Laban's: he took Leah, he brought her, and only then does Jacob act. The wayyiqtol in verse 24 (vayyitten, ‘and he gave’) is best read as an aside that supplies background, which is why some renderings use the pluperfect ‘had given’.
verses.history: Documents from ancient Mesopotamia show that a father could give his daughter slaves as part of her dowry, property that went with her into the marriage. Laban's gift of Zilpah to Leah, and later Bilhah to Rachel (verse 29), fits that practice, as does Rebekah's leaving home with her maids (24:61). In the next chapter these two women become mothers of four of Jacob's sons, and in 31:14-15 the sisters complain that their father sold them and spent what was paid.

verses.context: Morning reveals what the dark concealed. Jacob confronts Laban with three questions, and every one of them could have been put to Jacob by Isaac or Esau.
verses.grammar: "There was Leah" is vehinneh-hi le'ah, literally ‘and look, she was Leah’. The particle hinneh drops the reader into Jacob's discovery at dawn without any narrator's comment. His first question, mah-zot asita li ("What have you done to me?"), is the question others asked of his family: Pharaoh to Abram (12:18), Abimelech to Abraham (20:9) and to Isaac (26:10), and, in its first form, God to the woman in the garden (3:13). Now the grandson of Abraham asks it as the injured party. His final word, rimmitani, is a Piel perfect of ramah, ‘to deceive’, the root of the noun Isaac used of Jacob in 27:35.

theology.note: The verse shows sin returning on the sinner in kind. Jacob used darkness, disguise, and a father's blindness; Laban uses darkness, a bride who was probably veiled, and a groom's trust. Scripture calls this reaping what one sows (Galatians 6:7), and the narrator lets the symmetry speak without adding a moral.

God is not named in the deception, but the story's shape is not accidental. The same Lord who promised at Bethel to keep Jacob (28:15) also disciplines him, and Jacob's pain here becomes part of his reshaping into Israel.

verses.context: Laban answers with local custom and a new offer. He will give Rachel too, after Leah's wedding week, in exchange for seven more years. The deception becomes a bargain, and Laban gains another seven years of Jacob's skill with flocks.
verses.grammar: Laban's words carry a barb. Lo-ye'aseh khen bimqomenu, ‘it is not done so in our place’, stresses ‘our’: here, unlike wherever you come from, the younger does not go before the firstborn. The word for the older daughter is bekhirah, the feminine of bekhor, ‘firstborn’, the very status Jacob bought from Esau (25:31-34). ‘Complete this one's week’ (malle shevua zot) uses the demonstrative zot, ‘this one’, for Leah, and then again for Rachel (gam et-zot, ‘this one too’); Laban speaks of both daughters without their names, as goods in a trade. Shevua means a unit of seven, here the seven days of the wedding feast.
verses.history: A wedding celebration lasting seven days also appears in Samson's story (Judges 14:12, 17). Laban's custom of marrying the older daughter first cannot be confirmed from outside the text, but it is plausible, and his real offense is not the custom but concealing it for seven years.

verses.context: Jacob accepts. After one week he receives Rachel as well, and then he serves another seven years, this time after the wedding rather than before it. Rachel receives Bilhah as her maidservant. The section ends on the plain fact that will drive the next chapter: Jacob loved Rachel more.
verses.grammar: Vayyaas Ya'aqov ken ("Jacob did just that") is the language of compliance: the man who once dictated terms to Esau now simply does as he is told. Verse 30 uses gam (‘also’) twice: he went in ‘also’ to Rachel, and he loved ‘also’ Rachel more than Leah. The second gam is awkward in Hebrew and has been read two ways: either it simply adds Rachel to Leah as a wife he slept with, or it concedes that Jacob loved Leah too, only less. The comparative min (mille'ah, ‘more than Leah’) tells the reader Jacob's heart was divided, not empty toward Leah.

theology.note: Two sisters married to one man, one loved more than the other, is the arrangement Israel's law later forbids (Leviticus 18:18) and guards against (Deuteronomy 21:15-17, which protects the firstborn of an unloved wife). The verse shows the household that made those laws necessary.

verses.context: The LORD is named for the first time in the chapter, and his first act is to see the woman Jacob overlooked. The verse turns the story: Leah receives what the loved sister lacks, and Rachel joins Sarah and Rebekah as a barren matriarch.
verses.grammar: Vayyar YHWH ki senu'ah Le'ah ("When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved") puts God's seeing first, and the verb ra'ah will give Leah's firstborn his name in the next verse. Senu'ah is a passive participle of sane (‘hate’), used comparatively, as the chapter note explains. "He opened her womb" (vayyiftach et-rachmah) makes God the direct giver of conception, and the adjective aqarah ("barren") links Rachel to Sarah (11:30) and Rebekah (25:21), both of whom were also barren before God intervened.

theology.note: Conception is attributed to the LORD's act, not to chance or to human favor. The same God who opens Leah's womb will later remember Rachel and open hers (30:22), so both sisters' children come from his hand.

God's attention settles on the one who is not chosen by Jacob. The pattern of God choosing the overlooked, already seen in the choice of Isaac over Ishmael and of Jacob himself over Esau, runs here through a woman, and from her come Levi and Judah.

verses.context: Leah's first son is Reuben, and her explanation of the name tells her story in one breath: God has seen her misery, and surely now her husband will love her. It is the first of a series of naming speeches that will run through chapter 30.
verses.grammar: Reuben (re'uven) sounds like re'u ven, ‘see, a son’, and Leah's explanation plays on it with ra'ah YHWH be'onyi, "The LORD has seen my affliction". Biblical name explanations like this are usually sound plays rather than strict etymologies; the point is what the name reminds the family of. Oni ("affliction") is the word used when the LORD heard Hagar's affliction (16:11) and when he saw Israel's affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:7). The second clause, ki attah ye'ehavani ishi, is an imperfect of hope, ‘now my husband will love me’, and the whole chapter has told us he will not.

theology.note: Leah's first confession is that God sees affliction, the same word Scripture uses for Israel in slavery. Her hope for her husband's love is not yet met, but her grief has been noticed by God before anything in her circumstances changes.

verses.context: A second son, Simeon, named for God's hearing. Leah still speaks of herself as unloved, but her words now credit God with two gifts: he saw, and he heard.
verses.grammar: Simeon (shim'on) echoes shama (‘he has heard’). Leah repeats the participle from verse 31, senu'ah anokhi, ‘I am unloved’, now in her own mouth with the emphatic pronoun anokhi. The narrator's diagnosis has become her self-description. "This son as well" (gam-et-zeh) counts the gift: God has given a second one.

verses.context: The third son, Levi, carries Leah's hope that her husband will at last be joined to her. Three sons should have been enough to win his attachment; the next verse shows her hope beginning to turn elsewhere.
verses.grammar: Levi (levi) is explained by yillaveh, a Niphal of lavah, ‘to be joined, attached’: ‘this time my husband will be joined to me’. Numbers 18:2 and 18:4 later play on the same verb when Levi's tribe is told to ‘join’ Aaron in the service of the tabernacle, so the name that began as a wife's longing becomes a priestly calling. Unusually, the verb of naming is masculine, qara (‘he called’), where Leah names her other sons. It may be impersonal (hence the BSB's "he was named"), or it may mean Jacob named this son.
verses.text: The Hebrew has a masculine singular verb, literally ‘he called his name Levi’. Older English versions render it passively (the KJV's ‘was his name called Levi’), and the BSB follows with "he was named". Neither choice is wrong; a strictly literal rendering, ‘he named him’, would make Jacob the namer, while the passive leaves the namer open.

theology.note: Each of Leah's naming speeches measures her worth by her husband's response, and each is disappointed. The verse gives an honest picture of a marriage where one partner's longing goes unanswered, without pretending that more children fixed it.

verses.context: With her fourth son Leah stops speaking of her husband. She names Judah for praise of the LORD, and then she stops bearing, which sets up her sister's desperation in the next chapter.
verses.grammar: Hapa'am ("This time") links this verse to the one before: ‘this time my husband will be joined to me’ becomes ‘this time I will praise the LORD’. The verb odeh is a Hiphil imperfect of yadah, ‘to praise, give thanks, acknowledge’, and the name Judah (yehudah) is heard as its echo. Jacob's blessing in 49:8 plays on the same root: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you". The final clause, vatta'amod milledet, is literally ‘she stood still from bearing’, a pause rather than a permanent end, since Leah bears again in 30:17-21.

theology.note: The son Leah named for praise becomes the tribe of David's kings (Genesis 49:10) and of Jesus, whom Revelation calls the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Leah could not know this; her praise simply turned toward God before her circumstances did.

Leah's words move from petition and complaint to praise within four births. Scripture's psalms often make the same movement, and the verse shows praise offered while the underlying sorrow, an unloved marriage, remains.
